o: We scan the string and classify every character: vowels ('a','e','i','o','u') increment v, any other English letter increments c, and spaces/digits are ignored entirely. The score is integer division v // c, guarded so that c = 0 yields 0 instead of dividing by zero. In "cooear" we get v=4, c=2, score 2; in "axeyizou", v=5, c=3, floor(5/3)=1; in "au 123" there are letters but no consonants, so the guard triggers and the answer is 0. With length at most 100, a single linear pass is more than sufficient — no data structures or cleverness required.
k: Only alphabetic characters matter; digits and spaces are skipped.
Integer division naturally implements floor for non-negative counts.
The c = 0 case must be special-cased to avoid division by zero.

a.i: Walk the string once, maintaining two counters. A character contributes to exactly one counter only if it is a letter, and which counter depends on vowel membership. At the end apply the floor-division formula with the zero guard.
s: For each character: if it is a letter, increment v if it is a vowel, otherwise increment c.
Return v // c if c > 0, else 0.
a.t: O(n) — one pass over the string with O(1) work per character.

a.i: Functionally, filter the string down to its letters, then partition them into vowels and consonants using comprehensions/built-ins. It is the same computation expressed declaratively; useful when you want brevity.
s: Count vowels and consonants in the filtered list.
Apply the same floor-division formula with the zero guard.
a.t: O(n) — filtering and counting each touch every character once.

w: Either approach passes instantly; prefer the single-pass version in an interview for its O(1) space. Pitfalls: forgetting to ignore digits/spaces, treating 'y' as a vowel (it is not here), and crashing on c = 0. Follow-ups might ask for case-insensitivity (lowercase everything first) or streaming evaluation.
